description_full: Graco Inc. designs, manufactures, and markets systems and equipment used to move, measure, mix, control, dispense, and spray fluid and powder materials in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia Pacific. It operates through three segments: Contractor, Industrial and Expansion Markets. The Contractor segment provides sprayers to apply paint to walls and other structures; two-component proportioning systems to spray polyurethane foam and polyurea coatings; viscous coatings to roofs, markings on roads, parking lots, athletic fields, and floors; and high-performance volumetric and gravimetric dispense, mixing, and shaking equipment. The Industrial segment designs and manufactures liquid finishing and advanced fluid dispensing equipment; pumps to move chemicals, petroleum, food, and other fluids; and systems, components, and accessories for the automatic lubrication of bearings, gears, and generators; supplies equipment for equipment maintenance and vehicle servicing applications, as well as make powder finishing products and complete powder finishing systems. The Expansion Markets segment manufactures pumps for use in the semiconductor industry; high pressure and ultra-high-pressure valves used in the oil and natural gas industry; and environmental monitoring and remediation equipment that is used to conduct ground water sampling, ground water remediation, and for landfill liquid and gas management. Graco Inc. was incorporated in 1926 and is headquartered in Minneapolis, Minnesota.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 4K people. Revenue per employee of $508K ranks in the above the sector median among Industrials peers, with revenue growing 8%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $145K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $8K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 5× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (9/10).
financial_summary: Graco Inc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $11.6B market cap on $2.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 33% against a 9% cost of capital — a 24-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 53% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $638M in free cash flow — roughly 29 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.31× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 28% operating margin runs 19pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.51x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-2.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 24% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 26% and a beta of 0.90, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.35 vs 5y 0.89), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $125.2M traded a day, and interest is running hot at 1.5x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 31% in the 2020 crash, 27% in the 2022 bear market and 65% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $59.35 (margin of safety -22%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 41%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $49.54 to $72.70 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/FCF 18.2 vs 22.9 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-9%).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $83.29 on average, 15% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 33% clears the cost of capital of 9.2% by 24pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.34).
It runs a 53% gross margin and converts 29% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.31x.
ROE of 20% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.7% of revenue on R&D and 1.5% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $459.4M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 13.5, in the safe zone).
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 0.5 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
Working capital ties up about 175 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.4% over 3 years, 6.3% over 5 years and 5.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 14.6% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (2.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 33, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.8%), and institutions hold 94%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 1 sale over the past year, net $158K sold.
It returns 4.9% a year to shareholders (3.3% in buybacks and 1.6% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 38 consecutive years, raising it 9.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 4,400 employees, each generates about $508K of revenue, 1.4x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 7.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $145K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.4M (5x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
